scenes.tts: A sugar is added to a protein inside the E R of a cultured mammalian cell. Later, that sugar sits on the outside of the cell. Yet the protein never crossed a membrane on the way. So how does a sugar made inside the E R end up on the cell surface? The answer is one rule about the two faces of every membrane.

scenes.tts: A membrane is two sheets of lipid, and each sheet is called a leaflet. So every membrane has two faces. In the plasma membrane, E R, Golgi and endosomes, one face looks at the cytosol, the fluid that fills the cell outside the organelles. The other faces the outside of the cell, or the lumen inside an organelle such as the E R. Lipids and proteins slide sideways within their own leaflet, but cannot easily flip to the other.

scenes.tts: Take a protein with one membrane-spanning segment. Its N terminus is in the lumen of the E R. Its C terminus is in the cytosol, which makes it a single-pass type one protein. The N terminal domain carries a sugar, added in the lumen. This direction is set once, when the protein enters the E R membrane, usually through the translocon.

The N-terminal domain carries a sugar, added in the lumen. This direction is set once, when the protein enters the ER membrane, usually through the translocon.
scenes.visual: Large ER with the protein built piece by piece in its wall: spanning bar, N end and sugar in the lumen, C end in the cytosol, then the translocon outlined.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule: a lumen is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. A transport vesicle buds from one membrane and fuses with another. Its lumen is continuous first with the donor lumen, and then with the target lumen. Nothing crosses a membrane during the trip. The face that pointed at the cytosol keeps pointing at the cytosol.

scenes.tts: Follow the protein through the Golgi by vesicles, and the lumenal face stays lumenal. A secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane. Its lumen opens to the outside. The N terminus and the sugar now face the extracellular fluid. The C terminus stays in the cytosol.

scenes.visual: A vesicle leaves the Golgi, fuses with the plasma membrane; the vesicle lumen opens to the outside and the N end and sugar face the extracellular fluid; C end stays in the cytosol.

scenes.tts: Endocytosis pinches the plasma membrane inward, and the outside face becomes the lumen of an endosome. The N terminus and the sugar face that lumen, and the C terminus still faces the cytosol. At no step did the C terminus leave the cytosol. That is how a sugar made in the E R reaches the cell surface. Keep the rule: orientation is set once, at the E R, and traffic never flips it.
